title: Ice Cream 1.5L

drivers.name: Price increase (2.3%)
drivers.evidence: Price increase of 2.3% with no prior promotion at this level; historical price sensitivity suggests ~1.5% demand reduction.

adjustment.analysis: Thanksgiving week historically shows a 5% sales dip (x0.95 vs baseline), but the noise-adjusted effect is x1.0, indicating the dip is likely noise. The price increase to $6.56 (+2.3%) is a downside driver. No past promotion at this price level, and the historical promotion lift (x1.25 noise-adjusted) doesn't apply here. No promotion planned. The baseline already captures seasonal trends and recent demand. The uplift model’s neutral call is correct. No driver justifies a median shift. Confidence is high due to consistent noise-adjusted evidence.

brief:
PRODUCT: Ice Cream 1.5L | category Frozen | Store #12 (Austin, TX)
TARGET WEEK: 2026-11-23 to 2026-11-29 (7 weeks after the last week with sales data)

KNOWN PLAN FOR THE TARGET WEEK:
  events: Holiday: Thanksgiving (Thu)
  shelf price: 6.56 (+2.3% vs regular price 6.41)

STATISTICAL BASELINE (exponential smoothing of recent sales; it ignores events, promotions and prices):
  median 44.2 | 5%-95%: 11.7 - 74.8 | 10%-90%: 20.3 - 70.4

In the evidence below, 'vs baseline' = actual units / what this same baseline predicted for that week.
It is the multiplier that would have been right, so it maps directly onto median_multiplier.
This product's ordinary weeks already swing about +/-36% around the baseline, so a past effect smaller than that, seen only a few times, is mostly noise. The
'noise-adjusted estimate' is the effect shrunk toward x1.0 for that noise and the number of sightings.
